opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it started from a kind of frustration with how abstract everything felt. In computer science you spend a lot of time writing code that lives entirely inside the machine. You sort lists, you build data structures, you train a model on a dataset, and the results are numbers on a screen. That's intellectually satisfying, but I always had this itch to see the code *do* something in the physical world.

The first time I got to work with a real robot arm in a lab, it was a very humbling experience. You write what you think is a perfectly reasonable program to pick up an object, and then the robot misses by two centimeters, or the object slips, or the lighting changes and the perception falls apart. In simulation or on paper, everything works. In the real world, nothing works the first time. Strangely, that's what hooked me. It showed me how much we *don't* understand about something that a toddler does effortlessly, like picking up a cup.

There was also something very tangible and honest about it. When a robot succeeds, you see it with your own eyes. There's no ambiguity, no "well, the metric improved by half a percent." It either grasped the object or it didn't. That immediate feedback loop was really motivating for me as a young student.

And looking back, I think it planted the core question I've been chasing ever since: how do we get machines to learn and reason about the physical world the way humans do? Doing the hands-on work early made me appreciate that intelligence isn't just about computation. It's about acting in a messy, uncertain world. That's what drew me in, and it's never really let go.

r001.rationale: He contrasts abstract code and results on a screen with wanting to see code act in the physical world, then describes working with a robot arm.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it started with a bit of frustration. As an undergrad in computer science, so much of what I was doing lived entirely inside the screen. You write code, it runs, you get a number back, and that's it. There's a satisfaction in that, but it felt abstract, almost detached from the world I actually lived in.

Robotics was the first thing that made the code feel real. I remember the first time I got a robot arm to move the way I intended, and it was this very visceral moment. The algorithm wasn't just correct on paper, it was doing something in physical space, in front of me. And then of course it would fail in all these ways that I never would have predicted sitting at a terminal. The gripper would slip, the sensor would be noisy, the lighting would change, and suddenly my beautiful assumptions fell apart.

That gap is what hooked me. In pure software, you control the environment. In robotics, the world pushes back, and you have to deal with uncertainty, with messiness, with the fact that your model of the world is always a little bit wrong. I found that really humbling and really exciting at the same time. It forced me to think about perception, about planning, about learning, all together rather than as separate boxes.

I also think I was drawn to the sense that robotics was still an open problem. A lot of areas in CS felt quite mature by the time I got to them. But getting a robot to do something a child does effortlessly, like picking up a cup or stacking blocks, was still genuinely hard. That combination of a tangible, physical payoff and a wide-open intellectual frontier was pretty irresistible for a curious undergrad.

r001.rationale: He contrasts abstract, screen-only coding with the visceral satisfaction of getting a robot arm to move in physical space, identifying that physical result as part of what drew him to robotics.

astra-6.text: What drew me in was the connection between code and the physical world. As a computer science student, you spend a lot of time working with abstractions. With robotics, you can write a program and then watch a machine actually do something—and immediately see where your assumptions break down. I liked that hands-on process of building, testing, and figuring out why something didn’t work. It made the problems feel very tangible.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts working with abstractions with writing code and watching a machine act in the physical world, conveying the draw of making robotics produce real-world action.

sol-6.1.text: I was drawn to the idea that you could write a program and have it do something in the physical world. In computer science, so much of your work happens on a screen. With robotics, you have to connect that abstract reasoning to sensing, movement, and all the uncertainty of the real world. That combination of intellectual challenges and hands-on experimentation really appealed to me.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics lets a program act in the physical world and involves sensing and movement, contrasting this with computer science work on a screen.
